notes.overview: This chapter introduces how to write and balance chemical equations, and classifies chemical reactions into combination, decomposition, displacement, double displacement and oxidation-reduction reactions, along with the everyday phenomena of corrosion and rancidity that result from unwanted chemical change.

sections.title: 1. Chemical Equations and Balancing
sections.content: A chemical equation is the symbolic representation of a chemical reaction in terms of the formulae of the reactants and products; a balanced chemical equation has an equal number of atoms of each element on both the reactant and product sides, in accordance with the Law of Conservation of Mass, which states that mass can neither be created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction. Equations are balanced by adjusting coefficients (never subscripts) in front of formulae using the hit-and-trial method, and can be made more informative by mentioning the physical states of reactants and products (s, l, g, aq) and conditions like heat, catalyst or pressure above/below the arrow.

sections.title: 2. Combination Reactions
sections.content: A combination reaction is one in which two or more substances (elements or compounds) combine to form a single product, represented generally as A + B -> AB. Common examples include the burning of coal (C + O2 -> CO2), the formation of water from hydrogen and oxygen (2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O), and the slaking of lime, where calcium oxide reacts with water to form calcium hydroxide (CaO + H2O -> Ca(OH)2) - this last reaction is also exothermic, releasing a large amount of heat.

sections.title: 3. Decomposition Reactions
sections.content: A decomposition reaction is one in which a single compound breaks down into two or more simpler substances, represented as AB -> A + B; these reactions require energy input in the form of heat, light or electricity, and are therefore classified as thermal decomposition (e.g. heating calcium carbonate to give calcium oxide and carbon dioxide, CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2, the reaction used in the manufacture of cement), photodecomposition (e.g. silver chloride turning grey/black on exposure to sunlight, 2AgCl -> 2Ag + Cl2, used in black-and-white photography), or electrolytic decomposition (e.g. electrolysis of water into hydrogen and oxygen, 2H2O -> 2H2 + O2).

sections.title: 4. Displacement and Double Displacement Reactions
sections.content: A displacement reaction occurs when a more reactive element displaces a less reactive element from its compound, for example iron displacing copper from copper sulphate solution (Fe + CuSO4 -> FeSO4 + Cu), turning the blue solution pale green. A double displacement reaction involves the exchange of ions between two reactants, often producing an insoluble precipitate, for example sodium sulphate reacting with barium chloride to form a white precipitate of barium sulphate (Na2SO4 + BaCl2 -> BaSO4 + 2NaCl); reactions that form a precipitate are called precipitation reactions.

sections.title: 5. Oxidation and Reduction
sections.content: Oxidation is the addition of oxygen (or removal of hydrogen) to a substance, while reduction is the addition of hydrogen (or removal of oxygen); a reaction in which both oxidation and reduction occur simultaneously is called a redox reaction, since one reactant is oxidised while the other is reduced. For example, when copper(II) oxide reacts with hydrogen (CuO + H2 -> Cu + H2O), the copper oxide is reduced to copper (loses oxygen) while hydrogen is oxidised to water (gains oxygen).

sections.title: 6. Effects of Oxidation in Everyday Life: Corrosion and Rancidity
sections.content: Corrosion is the slow deterioration of metals caused by the action of air, moisture, or chemicals on their surface, forming compounds such as oxides - common examples are the rusting of iron (formation of reddish-brown hydrated iron oxide when iron is exposed to both moist air and oxygen together) and the tarnishing (blackening) of silver articles. Rancidity is the oxidation of fats and oils present in food, causing them to develop an unpleasant smell and taste when kept for a long time; it can be prevented by adding antioxidants to food, storing food in airtight containers, or packaging with nitrogen gas to displace oxygen.

key_terms.Balanced equation: A chemical equation with equal numbers of atoms of each element on both sides, consistent with the law of conservation of mass.
key_terms.Exothermic reaction: A reaction that releases heat energy to the surroundings.
key_terms.Endothermic reaction: A reaction that absorbs heat energy from the surroundings.
key_terms.Corrosion: The gradual destruction of metals by reaction with substances in their environment, such as moisture and oxygen.
key_terms.Rancidity: The oxidation of fats and oils in food, causing an unpleasant taste and smell.

important_facts: Law of Conservation of Mass: mass is neither created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction.
Rusting of iron needs both oxygen and moisture (water) to occur.
CaO + H2O -> Ca(OH)2 (slaking of lime) is a combination reaction and is exothermic.
2AgCl -> 2Ag + Cl2 (in sunlight) is a photodecomposition reaction, basis of black-and-white photography.
Redox reaction: one species is oxidised (loses electrons/gains oxygen) while another is reduced (gains electrons/loses oxygen) simultaneously.
exam_tips: Practice balancing equations and writing the physical states (s, l, g, aq) - a common 2-mark skill question.
Learn to identify the reaction type from a given equation - a frequent MCQ and 2-mark question type.
Rusting requires both air (oxygen) and water/moisture - a classic 2-mark 'what conditions are needed' question.

questions.explanation: 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O has equal numbers of H and O atoms on both sides.

questions.question: Rusting of iron occurs in the presence of:

questions.question: In the reaction CuO + H2 -> Cu + H2O, hydrogen is:
questions.explanation: Hydrogen gains oxygen to form water, so it is oxidised.

questions.question: CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2 (on heating) is an example of:
questions.explanation: Heat causes a single compound to break down into two products - thermal decomposition.

questions.question: What is rancidity? Suggest two ways to prevent it.

rubric.point: Rancidity is oxidation of fats/oils in food causing bad smell/taste
Prevented by antioxidants, airtight containers, or nitrogen packaging (any two)

questions.model_answer: Rancidity is the oxidation of fats and oils present in food, which gives the food an unpleasant smell and taste. It can be prevented by adding antioxidants to food, storing food in airtight containers, or packaging food with nitrogen gas to keep oxygen away.

questions.question: Define a combination reaction and give one example with its balanced equation.

rubric.point: Two or more substances combine to form a single product
Correct example with balanced equation, e.g. CaO + H2O -> Ca(OH)2

questions.model_answer: A combination reaction is one in which two or more substances combine to form a single new product. For example, calcium oxide reacts with water to form calcium hydroxide: CaO + H2O -> Ca(OH)2.

questions.question: Distinguish between displacement and double displacement reactions, giving one example of each.

rubric.point: Displacement: a more reactive element displaces a less reactive one from its compound
Double displacement: exchange of ions between two compounds, often forming a precipitate
Correct examples for both, e.g. Fe+CuSO4 and Na2SO4+BaCl2

questions.model_answer: In a displacement reaction, a more reactive element displaces a less reactive element from its compound, e.g. Fe + CuSO4 -> FeSO4 + Cu. In a double displacement reaction, two compounds exchange ions with each other, often forming an insoluble precipitate, e.g. Na2SO4 + BaCl2 -> BaSO4 + 2NaCl.

questions.question: What is corrosion? Explain with the example of rusting of iron, and state one method to prevent it.

rubric.point: Corrosion is the slow destruction of metals by reaction with air/moisture/chemicals around them
Rusting: iron reacts with oxygen and moisture to form hydrated iron oxide (rust)
Prevention method, e.g. painting, galvanising, oiling/greasing

questions.model_answer: Corrosion is the gradual deterioration of a metal due to the action of air, moisture or chemicals on its surface. Rusting of iron is a common example, where iron reacts with oxygen and moisture in the air to form hydrated iron oxide, commonly known as rust. Corrosion can be prevented by methods such as painting the metal surface, galvanising (coating with zinc), or applying oil/grease to keep out air and moisture.

questions.question: Explain, with a balanced chemical equation for each, the following types of chemical reactions: (a) combination reaction, (b) decomposition reaction, (c) displacement reaction, (d) double displacement reaction, (e) oxidation reaction.

rubric.point: Combination reaction defined with correct balanced equation
Decomposition reaction defined with correct balanced equation
Displacement reaction defined with correct balanced equation
Double displacement reaction defined with correct balanced equation
Oxidation reaction defined with correct example (gain of oxygen/loss of hydrogen)

questions.model_answer: (a) Combination reaction: two or more substances combine to form one product, e.g. CaO + H2O -> Ca(OH)2. (b) Decomposition reaction: a single compound breaks down into simpler substances, e.g. CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2 on heating. (c) Displacement reaction: a more reactive element displaces a less reactive one from its compound, e.g. Fe + CuSO4 -> FeSO4 + Cu. (d) Double displacement reaction: two compounds exchange ions, often forming a precipitate, e.g. Na2SO4 + BaCl2 -> BaSO4 + 2NaCl. (e) Oxidation reaction: a substance gains oxygen or loses hydrogen, e.g. when 2Cu + O2 -> 2CuO on heating, copper is oxidised to copper oxide.

questions.question: In a balanced chemical equation, the coefficients placed before formulae represent the:
options: Number of atoms of one element only
Number of molecules/moles of each substance
Mass of the substance in grams
Volume of the substance in litres
questions.explanation: Coefficients indicate the relative number of molecules or moles of each reactant/product.

questions.question: The reaction 2AgCl -> 2Ag + Cl2 taking place in sunlight is an example of:
questions.explanation: Light energy causes silver chloride to decompose - a photodecomposition reaction, used in black-and-white photography.

questions.question: Which type of decomposition reaction is used to split water into hydrogen and oxygen?
questions.explanation: Passing electricity through water decomposes it into hydrogen and oxygen - electrolytic decomposition.

questions.question: When solutions of sodium sulphate and barium chloride are mixed, a white precipitate is formed. This reaction is an example of a:
questions.explanation: Ions are exchanged between the two compounds, forming insoluble barium sulphate - a precipitation/double displacement reaction.

questions.question: The slaking of lime (CaO + H2O -> Ca(OH)2) is a combination reaction that is:
questions.explanation: Slaking of lime releases a large amount of heat, making it exothermic.

questions.question: When a magnesium ribbon burns in air to form magnesium oxide, this is an example of a:
questions.explanation: Magnesium combines with oxygen to form a single product, magnesium oxide - a combination reaction.

questions.question: While balancing a chemical equation, it is correct to change the:
options: Coefficient in front of a formula
questions.explanation: Only coefficients (never subscripts, which would change the substance itself) may be adjusted to balance an equation.

questions.question: Silver articles turn black over time when exposed to air. This is due to:
questions.explanation: Silver reacts slowly with substances in the air and tarnishes (blackens) - a form of corrosion.

questions.question: In the reaction Pb(NO3)2 + 2KI -> PbI2 + 2KNO3, a yellow precipitate of lead iodide is formed. This is an example of a:
questions.explanation: Ions are exchanged between lead nitrate and potassium iodide, forming an insoluble yellow precipitate - a double displacement reaction.

questions.question: Which of the following substances is added to fats and oils in packaged food to prevent rancidity?
questions.explanation: Antioxidants slow down the oxidation of fats and oils, preventing rancidity.

questions.question: 2KClO3 (heated with MnO2 catalyst) -> 2KCl + 3O2 is an example of a:
options: Reaction that is not a decomposition reaction
questions.explanation: Heat causes potassium chlorate to break down into simpler substances - thermal decomposition.

questions.question: A reaction in which heat is absorbed from the surroundings is called a(n):
questions.explanation: Endothermic reactions absorb heat energy from their surroundings as they proceed.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT correct about a balanced chemical equation?
options: The number of atoms of each element is equal on both sides
It follows the Law of Conservation of Mass
The number of molecules of reactants must equal the number of molecules of products
Coefficients may be adjusted, but not subscripts
questions.explanation: A balanced equation requires equal atoms of each element on both sides, not equal numbers of molecules.

questions.question: What is a redox reaction? Give one example.

rubric.point: A reaction in which oxidation and reduction occur simultaneously
Correct example, e.g. CuO + H2 -> Cu + H2O (CuO reduced, H2 oxidised)

questions.model_answer: A redox reaction is one in which oxidation and reduction take place simultaneously - one reactant is oxidised while the other is reduced. For example, in CuO + H2 -> Cu + H2O, copper oxide is reduced to copper while hydrogen is oxidised to water.

questions.question: What happens when ferrous sulphate crystals are heated strongly? Write the observation and the equation.

rubric.point: Green ferrous sulphate crystals turn into a reddish-brown residue and give off gases with a smell of burning sulphur
Correct equation: 2FeSO4 -> Fe2O3 + SO2 + SO3

questions.model_answer: On heating, green ferrous sulphate crystals lose water and decompose into reddish-brown ferric oxide, along with sulphur dioxide and sulphur trioxide gases, which have a characteristic pungent smell: 2FeSO4 -> Fe2O3 + SO2 + SO3.

questions.question: Distinguish between exothermic and endothermic reactions with one example each.

rubric.point: Exothermic reactions release heat, e.g. slaking of lime or respiration
Endothermic reactions absorb heat, e.g. thermal decomposition of calcium carbonate

questions.model_answer: An exothermic reaction releases heat energy to the surroundings, for example the slaking of lime (CaO + H2O -> Ca(OH)2). An endothermic reaction absorbs heat energy from the surroundings, for example the thermal decomposition of calcium carbonate (CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2) on strong heating.

questions.question: Why should physical states of reactants and products be mentioned in a chemical equation? Give an example.

rubric.point: Makes the equation more informative/complete by showing whether a substance is solid, liquid, gas or dissolved
Correct example using s/l/g/aq notation

questions.model_answer: Mentioning the physical states of reactants and products makes a chemical equation more informative, since it shows whether each substance is a solid, liquid, gas or in aqueous solution. For example: CaCO3(s) -> CaO(s) + CO2(g).

questions.question: What happens when dilute hydrochloric acid is added to iron filings? Write the balanced equation.

rubric.point: Hydrogen gas is evolved and iron chloride (a salt) is formed - a displacement reaction
Correct equation: Fe + 2HCl -> FeCl2 + H2

questions.model_answer: Iron filings react with dilute hydrochloric acid to displace hydrogen gas and form iron(II) chloride, a displacement reaction: Fe + 2HCl -> FeCl2 + H2.

questions.question: Explain thermal decomposition, photodecomposition and electrolytic decomposition, giving one example of each.

rubric.point: Thermal decomposition uses heat, e.g. CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2
Photodecomposition uses light, e.g. 2AgCl -> 2Ag + Cl2 in sunlight
Electrolytic decomposition uses electricity, e.g. 2H2O -> 2H2 + O2

questions.model_answer: Thermal decomposition occurs on heating, e.g. CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2. Photodecomposition occurs in the presence of light, e.g. 2AgCl -> 2Ag + Cl2 when exposed to sunlight. Electrolytic decomposition occurs when electricity is passed through a compound, e.g. 2H2O -> 2H2 + O2.

questions.question: What is corrosion? Explain the conditions needed for rusting of iron, and state two methods to prevent it.

rubric.point: Corrosion is the slow destruction of a metal by reaction with substances around it (air, moisture, chemicals)
Rusting needs both oxygen and moisture together to form hydrated iron oxide
Prevention methods, e.g. painting, galvanising, oiling/greasing (any two)

questions.model_answer: Corrosion is the gradual destruction of a metal due to reaction with substances present around it, such as air, moisture or chemicals. Rusting of iron specifically requires the presence of both oxygen and moisture together, which combine with iron to form hydrated iron oxide (rust). It can be prevented by painting the surface, galvanising it with zinc, or applying oil or grease to keep out air and moisture.

questions.question: A magnesium ribbon is burnt in air, both before and after cleaning it with sandpaper. State the observations and explain the reason for any difference, with the equation.

rubric.point: An uncleaned ribbon has a layer of magnesium oxide on its surface, which makes it harder to ignite and burn well
After cleaning with sandpaper, the ribbon burns with a bright/dazzling white flame
Correct equation: 2Mg + O2 -> 2MgO

questions.model_answer: Magnesium reacts slowly with atmospheric oxygen even at room temperature, forming a thin protective layer of magnesium oxide on the surface of the ribbon, which can prevent it from burning well. Cleaning the ribbon with sandpaper removes this oxide layer, so the cleaned ribbon burns with a bright, dazzling white flame to form magnesium oxide: 2Mg + O2 -> 2MgO.

questions.question: What is a precipitation reaction? Explain with the example of silver nitrate reacting with sodium chloride, including the balanced equation.

rubric.point: A precipitation reaction forms an insoluble solid (precipitate) when two solutions are mixed
Correct equation: AgNO3 + NaCl -> AgCl + NaNO3
AgCl formed is a white, insoluble precipitate

questions.model_answer: A precipitation reaction is one in which an insoluble solid, called a precipitate, is formed when two solutions are mixed. For example, when silver nitrate solution reacts with sodium chloride solution, a white insoluble precipitate of silver chloride is formed: AgNO3 + NaCl -> AgCl + NaNO3.

questions.question: What is the difference between a combination reaction and a decomposition reaction? Explain using suitable examples.

rubric.point: Combination reaction: two or more substances combine to form a single product, e.g. CaO + H2O -> Ca(OH)2
Decomposition reaction: a single compound breaks down into two or more simpler substances, e.g. CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2
Decomposition reactions are essentially the reverse of combination reactions

questions.model_answer: In a combination reaction, two or more substances combine to form a single product, e.g. CaO + H2O -> Ca(OH)2. In a decomposition reaction, a single compound breaks down into two or more simpler substances, e.g. CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2 on heating. Decomposition reactions can be thought of as essentially the reverse of combination reactions.

questions.question: Explain the following, giving a suitable example and balanced equation for each: (a) an exothermic reaction, (b) an endothermic reaction, (c) a precipitation reaction, (d) a photodecomposition reaction, (e) a reaction that evolves a gas which turns lime water milky.

rubric.point: Exothermic reaction with example, e.g. CaO + H2O -> Ca(OH)2
Endothermic reaction with example, e.g. CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2
Precipitation reaction with example, e.g. Na2SO4 + BaCl2 -> BaSO4 + NaCl
Photodecomposition reaction with example, e.g. 2AgCl -> 2Ag + Cl2
Reaction evolving CO2 that turns lime water milky, e.g. Na2CO3 + 2HCl -> 2NaCl + H2O + CO2

questions.model_answer: (a) Exothermic reaction releases heat, e.g. CaO + H2O -> Ca(OH)2. (b) Endothermic reaction absorbs heat, e.g. CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2 on strong heating. (c) A precipitation reaction forms an insoluble solid, e.g. Na2SO4 + BaCl2 -> BaSO4 + 2NaCl. (d) A photodecomposition reaction is triggered by light, e.g. 2AgCl -> 2Ag + Cl2 in sunlight. (e) Reaction of a carbonate with an acid evolves carbon dioxide gas, which turns lime water milky, e.g. Na2CO3 + 2HCl -> 2NaCl + H2O + CO2.

questions.topic: Applications of chemical reactions in daily life
questions.question: Explain any five ways in which chemical reactions affect our everyday life, giving one relevant example for each (you may refer to corrosion, rancidity, respiration, digestion of food, or manufacture of useful substances).

rubric.point: Corrosion damages metal objects over time, e.g. rusting of iron
Rancidity spoils the taste/smell of fatty foods due to oxidation
Respiration is an oxidation reaction in our body that releases energy from food
Cement is manufactured using the thermal decomposition of limestone (calcium carbonate)
Digestion of food involves the breakdown of large food molecules into simpler substances

questions.model_answer: Chemical reactions affect everyday life in many ways: corrosion gradually damages metal objects, as seen in the rusting of iron; rancidity spoils the taste and smell of fatty foods due to oxidation of the fats and oils; respiration in our bodies is an oxidation reaction that releases the energy we need from food; the manufacture of cement relies on the thermal decomposition of limestone into calcium oxide and carbon dioxide; and digestion of food is the breakdown of large, complex food molecules into simpler substances that our body can absorb.

questions.topic: Case study - thermal decomposition and corrosion of calcium carbonate (adapted from CBSE Question Bank material)
questions.passage: A student heats calcium carbonate (CaCO3) in a test tube; on heating, it decomposes into calcium oxide (CaO) and carbon dioxide (CO2) gas. Calcium carbonate is also the main component of marble statues and monuments, which are known to corrode when they repeatedly come into contact with acidic pollutants in rainwater.

subquestions.question: What type of chemical reaction occurs when CaCO3 is heated?
subquestions.explanation: A single compound (CaCO3) breaks down into two simpler products (CaO and CO2) - this is a thermal decomposition reaction.

subquestions.question: Marble monuments corrode on repeated contact with polluted rainwater mainly because:
options: polluted rainwater is acidic and reacts with the calcium carbonate
polluted rainwater is basic and reacts with the calcium carbonate
calcium carbonate simply dissolves in any water, polluted or not
the marble absorbs carbon dioxide directly from the air
subquestions.explanation: Polluted rainwater (acid rain) contains dissolved acidic gases and is acidic; it reacts with and slowly dissolves the calcium carbonate in marble, causing corrosion.

subquestions.question: Write the balanced chemical equation for the thermal decomposition of calcium carbonate, and state one everyday use of the calcium oxide produced.

rubric.point: CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2 (on heating), already balanced (1 Ca, 1 C, 3 O on each side)
Calcium oxide (quicklime) is used e.g. in manufacturing cement, in whitewashing, or in neutralising acidic soil

subquestions.model_answer: CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2 (on heating). This equation is already balanced: 1 calcium, 1 carbon and 3 oxygen atoms appear on each side. The calcium oxide (quicklime) produced is commonly used in manufacturing cement, in whitewashing buildings, and in neutralising acidic soil in agriculture.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): The reaction CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2 is an example of a decomposition reaction.
Reason (R): In a decomposition reaction, a single reactant breaks down into two or more simpler products.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
questions.explanation: Both statements are true, and R correctly states the general definition that makes A a decomposition reaction.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Rusting of iron is an example of a decomposition reaction.
Reason (R): Rusting involves the combination of iron with oxygen and moisture from the air to form hydrated iron(III) oxide.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
questions.explanation: Rusting is a COMBINATION (oxidation) reaction, not a decomposition reaction, so A is false. R correctly describes what happens during rusting.

questions.topic: Case study - redox reaction in bleaching powder manufacture (adapted from CBSE Question Bank)
questions.passage: The reaction between manganese dioxide (MnO2) and hydrochloric acid (HCl) releases a gas with bleaching abilities: MnO2 + 4HCl -> MnCl2 + Cl2 + 2H2O.

subquestions.question: The chemical reaction between MnO2 and HCl is an example of a:
subquestions.explanation: Manganese goes from +4 to +2 (reduced) while chlorine goes from -1 to 0 (oxidised) - both oxidation and reduction occur together, making this a redox reaction.

subquestions.question: In this reaction, chlorine gas released can react with dry Ca(OH)2 to form:
subquestions.explanation: Chlorine gas reacts with dry slaked lime (Ca(OH)2) to form bleaching powder (CaOCl2), a standard industrial process.

subquestions.question: Identify which substance is oxidised and which is reduced in this reaction, and what would happen if dry HCl gas were used instead of its aqueous solution. Explain your answer.

rubric.point: MnO2 is reduced (Mn: +4 to +2) and HCl is oxidised (Cl: -1 to 0, forming Cl2)
With dry HCl gas (no water), the reaction would not occur, since acids show their characteristic reactivity only when ionised in aqueous solution
keywords: dry HCl - reaction will not occur

subquestions.model_answer: MnO2 is getting reduced (manganese goes from +4 to +2), while HCl is getting oxidised (chlorine goes from -1 to 0, forming Cl2 gas). If dry HCl gas were used instead of its aqueous solution, the reaction would not occur - acids only show their characteristic behaviour (ionising to release H+/H3O+ ions) when dissolved in water, so dry HCl gas alone cannot drive this reaction.

questions.topic: Identifying reaction type from a general equation
questions.question: A single displacement reaction is represented below: PQ + R -> PR + Q. Which of the following is true about the reactants and products?
options: R forms a cation in the product, and PR is more stable than PQ
R forms a cation in the product, and PR is less stable than PQ
R forms an anion in the product, and PR is more stable than PQ
R forms an anion in the product, and PR is less stable than PQ
questions.explanation: In a displacement reaction, the more reactive element (R) displaces the less reactive element (Q) from its compound because R forms a more stable bond/compound with P. Since R takes Q's place (typically as the electronegative/anionic partner in this generic pairing), the product PR is more stable than the original PQ - that greater stability is exactly why the reaction proceeds.

questions.question:
Some types of chemical reactions are: decomposition, combination, displacement, double displacement. Which two of the following reactions are of the SAME type?
P) AgNO3 + NaCl -> AgCl + NaNO3
Q) Mg + 2HCl -> MgCl2 + H2
R) CH4 + 2O2 -> CO2 + 2H2O
S) 2KOH + H2SO4 -> K2SO4 + 2H2O
questions.explanation: P (AgNO3 + NaCl -> AgCl + NaNO3) and S (2KOH + H2SO4 -> K2SO4 + 2H2O, a neutralisation) are both double displacement reactions, where the ions of the two reactants exchange partners. Q is a displacement reaction (Mg displaces H from HCl) and R is a combination reaction (combustion).

Red-coloured copper is oxidised to red-coloured copper(I) oxide
Red-coloured copper is reduced to black-coloured copper(II) oxide
Red-coloured copper is oxidised to black-coloured copper(II) oxide

questions.question: In the balanced chemical equation xFe(s) + yH2O(g) -> Fe3O4(s) + 4H2(g), what is the ratio x:y of the reactant coefficients?
questions.explanation: The balanced equation is 3Fe(s) + 4H2O(g) -> Fe3O4(s) + 4H2(g), so x:y = 3:4.

questions.topic: Identifying parent acid and base of salts
questions.question: Salts are formed by the neutralisation reaction between an acid and a base. For each salt, name the parent base and parent acid: (1) Ammonium chloride, NH4Cl. (2) Copper sulphate, formed from Cu(OH)2.

rubric.point: Ammonium chloride (NH4Cl) is formed from ammonium hydroxide (NH4OH) as the base and hydrochloric acid (HCl) as the acid
Copper sulphate is formed from copper hydroxide, Cu(OH)2, as the base and sulphuric acid (H2SO4) as the acid

questions.model_answer: Ammonium chloride (NH4Cl) is the salt of the base ammonium hydroxide (NH4OH) and the acid hydrochloric acid (HCl). Copper sulphate is the salt of the base copper hydroxide, Cu(OH)2, and the acid sulphuric acid (H2SO4).

questions.topic: Redox roles in the reaction of iron with steam
questions.question:
Assertion (A): In the reaction 3Fe(s) + 4H2O(g) -> Fe3O4(s) + 4H2(g), iron is oxidised and water acts as the oxidising agent.
Reason (R): Water is reduced in this reaction, as the hydrogen in water (oxidation state +1) is converted to hydrogen gas (oxidation state 0).
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
questions.explanation: Both statements are true, and R explains A: iron metal (0) is oxidised to Fe3O4 (losing electrons), while the hydrogen atoms in water are reduced from the +1 oxidation state down to 0 as hydrogen gas - since water is the species that gets reduced, it is, by definition, the oxidising agent in this reaction.

questions.topic: Decomposition of potassium chlorate is endothermic
questions.question:
Assertion (A): The reaction 2KClO3(s) --[heat, MnO2 catalyst]--> 2KCl(s) + 3O2(g), used to prepare oxygen gas in the laboratory, is a decomposition reaction.
Reason (R): This decomposition reaction requires continuous heat input to proceed, making it endothermic in nature.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
questions.explanation: Both statements are true, and R correctly adds relevant detail to A: potassium chlorate breaking down into potassium chloride and oxygen is indeed a decomposition reaction (one compound breaking into two products), and since it needs a continuous supply of heat to keep proceeding, it is an endothermic decomposition.

questions.topic: Case study - thermal decomposition of copper(II) nitrate

notes.overview: This chapter studies the chemical properties of acids and bases, how they can be identified using indicators, what happens when they neutralise each other, the pH scale for measuring acidity/alkalinity, and important salts encountered in daily life along with the water of crystallisation.

sections.title: 1. Acids and Bases: Properties and Indicators
sections.content: Acids are substances that taste sour and turn blue litmus red, while bases are substances that taste bitter, feel soapy and turn red litmus blue; a base that is soluble in water is specifically called an alkali. Indicators are substances that change colour depending on whether they are put in an acidic or basic solution - common ones include litmus (red in acid, blue in base), phenolphthalein (colourless in acid, pink in base) and methyl orange (red in acid, yellow in base); olfactory indicators like onion or vanilla extract change smell in the presence of a base.
keywords: bases bitter soapy red litmus blue
sections.video_title: Indicators - Acids, Bases and Salts (Magnet Brains)

sections.title: 2. Reaction of Acids and Bases with Metals
sections.content: When acids react with active metals such as zinc, magnesium or iron, they produce a salt and hydrogen gas, for example zinc reacting with dilute sulphuric acid: Zn + H2SO4 -> ZnSO4 + H2; the evolved hydrogen gas can be tested with a burning matchstick, which produces a characteristic 'pop' sound. Similarly, when bases react with metals like zinc, they also produce hydrogen gas along with a salt, e.g. 2NaOH + Zn -> Na2ZnO2 (sodium zincate) + H2.

sections.title: 3. Reaction of Acids and Bases with Carbonates and Neutralisation
sections.content: Acids react with metal carbonates and bicarbonates to produce a salt, water and carbon dioxide gas, e.g. Na2CO3 + 2HCl -> 2NaCl + H2O + CO2, and the CO2 evolved turns lime water milky. Neutralisation is the reaction between an acid and a base that produces a salt and water, with the heat evolved making it an exothermic reaction: NaOH + HCl -> NaCl + H2O; this reaction is used to treat acidity in the stomach (using antacids like milk of magnesia) and to treat soil acidity (using slaked lime).

sections.title: 4. The pH Scale
sections.content: The pH scale (0-14) is used to measure the concentration of hydrogen ions in a solution, and hence how acidic or basic it is: a pH of exactly 7 is neutral (as in pure water), values less than 7 indicate an acidic solution (the lower the value, the more strongly acidic), and values greater than 7 indicate a basic solution (the higher the value, the more strongly basic). The pH of a solution is important in everyday life - for example, the pH of human blood and saliva must remain close to neutral for the body to function properly, tooth decay begins when the pH of the mouth falls below 5.5, and plants and animals are sensitive to pH changes in soil and water.
sections.video_title: pH Value of Acidic and Basic Solutions (Magnet Brains)

sections.title: 5. Important Salts and Water of Crystallisation
sections.content: Common salt (sodium chloride, NaCl) is the source of several important chemicals: electrolysis of its solution (brine) gives sodium hydroxide, chlorine and hydrogen (chlor-alkali process); it is also used to make washing soda (Na2CO3.10H2O) and baking soda (NaHCO3, sodium hydrogen carbonate, used in cooking and as a mild antacid). Water of crystallisation is the fixed number of water molecules chemically bound in one formula unit of a salt crystal, e.g. copper sulphate crystals (CuSO4.5H2O, blue vitriol) contain 5 water molecules and gypsum (CaSO4.1/2H2O) is used to make Plaster of Paris by heating.

key_terms.Indicator: A substance that changes colour or smell depending on whether it is added to an acid or a base.
key_terms.Neutralisation: The reaction between an acid and a base to produce a salt and water, releasing heat.
key_terms.pH scale: A scale from 0 to 14 that measures how acidic or basic a solution is, based on hydrogen ion concentration.
key_terms.Water of crystallisation: The fixed number of water molecules present in one formula unit of a salt.
key_terms.Olfactory indicator: A substance whose smell changes in acidic or basic media, such as onion or vanilla extract.

important_facts: Acid + Metal -> Salt + Hydrogen gas (tested with a burning matchstick giving a pop sound).
Acid + Metal carbonate -> Salt + Water + Carbon dioxide (turns lime water milky).
Neutralisation: Acid + Base -> Salt + Water (exothermic).
pH < 7 acidic, pH = 7 neutral, pH > 7 basic.
Baking soda = NaHCO3; Washing soda = Na2CO3.10H2O; Plaster of Paris made from gypsum (CaSO4.1/2H2O).
exam_tips: Learn the standard test for hydrogen gas (burning matchstick, pop sound) and for carbon dioxide gas (turns lime water milky) - common in 2-mark practical-based questions.
Be able to explain everyday uses of neutralisation (antacids, soil treatment) - a recurring 3-mark question.
Memorise the formulas and common/chemical names of baking soda, washing soda, and Plaster of Paris.

questions.model_answer: A neutralisation reaction is the reaction between an acid and a base that produces a salt and water, and releases heat. An everyday example is taking an antacid such as milk of magnesia to neutralise excess acid in the stomach and relieve acidity.

questions.question: Explain the importance of pH in everyday life with three examples.

rubric.point: pH of blood/body fluids must stay close to neutral for the body to function properly
Tooth decay starts when mouth pH falls below 5.5 due to bacterial action on food
Plants/crops and aquatic life are sensitive to soil/water pH; farmers adjust soil pH using lime or other substances

questions.model_answer: The pH of our body fluids, such as blood, must remain close to neutral for normal functioning; even a small change can cause serious problems. Tooth decay starts when the pH inside the mouth falls below 5.5, as bacteria acting on food particles produce acids that attack the enamel. Plants and aquatic organisms are also sensitive to pH - crops grow best within a specific soil pH range, and farmers may add substances like lime to correct overly acidic soil, while a sudden change in the pH of a pond or lake can harm fish and other aquatic life.

questions.question: Name the salt used to make washing soda and baking soda, write their chemical formulas, and give one use of each.

rubric.point: Washing soda: Na2CO3.10H2O, used for washing clothes/glass and soap industry
Baking soda: NaHCO3, used in cooking and as a mild antacid
Both are derived from common salt (sodium chloride)

questions.model_answer: Washing soda, sodium carbonate decahydrate (Na2CO3.10H2O), is used in the manufacture of glass, soap and for washing clothes. Baking soda, sodium hydrogen carbonate (NaHCO3), is used in cooking (as an ingredient in baking powder) and as a mild antacid to relieve acidity. Both washing soda and baking soda are prepared from common salt (sodium chloride).

questions.question: Explain what happens when (a) an acid reacts with a metal, (b) an acid reacts with a metal carbonate, (c) an acid reacts with a base, giving a balanced equation for each. Also explain the pH scale and state whether the pH of an acidic solution is less than or greater than 7.

rubric.point: Acid + metal -> salt + hydrogen, with correct equation
Acid + carbonate -> salt + water + carbon dioxide, with correct equation
Acid + base -> salt + water (neutralisation), with correct equation
pH scale explained as 0-14, measuring hydrogen ion concentration

questions.model_answer: (a) When an acid reacts with an active metal, it produces a salt and hydrogen gas, e.g. Zn + H2SO4 -> ZnSO4 + H2. (b) When an acid reacts with a metal carbonate, it produces a salt, water and carbon dioxide gas, e.g. Na2CO3 + 2HCl -> 2NaCl + H2O + CO2. (c) When an acid reacts with a base, a neutralisation reaction occurs, producing a salt and water, e.g. NaOH + HCl -> NaCl + H2O. The pH scale ranges from 0 to 14 and measures the concentration of hydrogen ions in a solution, indicating how acidic or basic it is. A solution with a pH less than 7 is acidic, a pH of exactly 7 is neutral, and a pH greater than 7 is basic.

questions.model_answer: An alkali is a base that is soluble in water. Examples include sodium hydroxide (NaOH), potassium hydroxide (KOH) and calcium hydroxide (Ca(OH)2).

questions.question: Why should we not add water to a concentrated acid directly? Explain the correct method of diluting an acid.

rubric.point: Dilution of a concentrated acid is highly exothermic and can cause spattering/splashing that may burn the skin

questions.model_answer: Adding water directly to a concentrated acid is dangerous because the process is highly exothermic; the heat generated can cause the mixture to spatter and cause burns. The safe method is to add the acid slowly to water with constant stirring, not the other way around, so the heat is safely absorbed by the larger volume of water.

Basic solution has pH greater than 7, example: soap solution or baking soda solution

questions.model_answer: The chlor-alkali process is the electrolysis of a concentrated solution (brine) of sodium chloride, producing three useful products: sodium hydroxide (used in making soaps and detergents), chlorine gas (used in disinfectants and PVC manufacture), and hydrogen gas (used as a fuel).

questions.topic: Role of water in acidic behaviour
questions.question: Explain why an aqueous solution of an acid conducts electricity and turns blue litmus red, while dry HCl gas does not show these properties. What does this indicate about the role of water?

rubric.point: Acids ionise/dissociate to produce H+ (hydronium) ions only in the presence of water
These ions are responsible for acidic behaviour, including conducting electricity and turning litmus red
Dry HCl gas has no free ions, so it does not show acidic properties; this shows water is essential for acidic character

questions.model_answer: An acid shows its acidic properties, such as conducting electricity and turning blue litmus red, only when dissolved in water, because water helps the acid ionise and release H+ ions. Dry HCl gas has no free ions and therefore does not turn dry litmus paper red or conduct electricity. This shows that the presence of water is essential for a substance to display acidic behaviour.

questions.question: What is water of crystallisation? Explain with reference to copper sulphate crystals (blue vitriol), including what happens when they are heated.

rubric.point: Water of crystallisation is the fixed number of water molecules chemically bound in one formula unit of a salt crystal
Copper sulphate crystals (CuSO4.5H2O) contain 5 water molecules, giving them their blue colour
On heating, the crystals lose water and turn white (anhydrous copper sulphate); adding water restores the blue colour

questions.model_answer: Water of crystallisation is the fixed number of water molecules chemically combined in one formula unit of a salt. Copper sulphate crystals, CuSO4.5H2O, contain 5 molecules of water of crystallisation, which give the crystals their characteristic blue colour. On strong heating, the crystals lose this water and turn into white anhydrous copper sulphate; adding water back to the white powder restores the blue colour.

questions.question: List three differences between acids and bases based on their taste, effect on litmus, and reaction with metals.

rubric.point: Taste: acids taste sour, bases taste bitter
Litmus: acids turn blue litmus red, bases turn red litmus blue
Reaction with metals: acids react with active metals to release hydrogen gas; only some bases react with metals like zinc/aluminium to release hydrogen

questions.model_answer: Acids taste sour while bases taste bitter. Acids turn blue litmus paper red, whereas bases turn red litmus paper blue. Acids readily react with active metals to release hydrogen gas and form a salt, while only some bases (like sodium hydroxide) react with certain metals such as zinc or aluminium to release hydrogen gas.

questions.question: (a) Define pH and state the pH range for acidic, neutral and basic solutions. (b) Explain the role of pH in the digestive system and in tooth decay. (c) Why is rainwater with pH below 5.6 called acid rain, and what harm can it cause?

rubric.point: pH is a scale (0-14) that measures hydrogen ion concentration; pH<7 acidic, pH=7 neutral, pH>7 basic
Stomach produces hydrochloric acid to help digest food; body fluids like blood must stay close to neutral pH
Tooth decay starts when mouth pH falls below 5.5 due to bacterial acids attacking enamel
Acid rain forms when rainwater pH falls below 5.6 due to dissolved acidic gases
Acid rain harms plants, buildings/monuments and aquatic life

questions.model_answer: (a) pH is a scale from 0 to 14 that measures the concentration of hydrogen ions in a solution; a pH below 7 is acidic, exactly 7 is neutral, and above 7 is basic. (b) Our stomach secretes hydrochloric acid to help digest food, and body fluids such as blood must remain close to neutral pH for the body to function properly. Tooth decay starts when the pH inside the mouth falls below 5.5, as bacteria acting on leftover food produce acids that attack the tooth enamel. (c) Rainwater with a pH below 5.6 is called acid rain, caused by acidic gases dissolving in atmospheric moisture; it can damage plants, corrode buildings and monuments, and harm aquatic life in rivers and lakes.

questions.question: Explain the following with examples: (a) an alkali, (b) a salt, (c) the chlor-alkali process, (d) washing soda and its uses, (e) Plaster of Paris and its use.

rubric.point: Alkali: a water-soluble base, e.g. NaOH
Salt: the compound formed when an acid reacts with a base, e.g. NaCl
Chlor-alkali process: electrolysis of brine giving NaOH, Cl2, H2
Washing soda: Na2CO3.10H2O, used in glass/soap manufacture and for washing
Plaster of Paris: made by heating gypsum, used to set fractured bones/making moulds

questions.model_answer: (a) An alkali is a base that is soluble in water, such as sodium hydroxide. (b) A salt is the compound formed when an acid reacts with a base, such as sodium chloride formed from HCl and NaOH. (c) The chlor-alkali process is the electrolysis of concentrated brine, producing sodium hydroxide, chlorine and hydrogen. (d) Washing soda (Na2CO3.10H2O) is used in the manufacture of glass and soap, and for washing clothes. (e) Plaster of Paris is made by heating gypsum to partially remove its water of crystallisation, and is widely used to set fractured bones and to make decorative moulds.

subquestions.explanation: A base (the antacid) reacting with an acid to relieve acidity is a classic example of a neutralisation reaction.

subquestions.question: The stomach's gastric juice is naturally acidic. Its pH is most likely to be around:

questions.topic: Case study - detergent pollution and pH (adapted from CBSE Question Bank)
questions.passage: High phosphate content in wastewater, largely from detergents used in dyeing industries, laundries and households, causes toxic frothing in rivers like the Yamuna. Parts of such rivers have been labelled 'dead' because there is not enough dissolved oxygen left for aquatic life to survive.

subquestions.question: If the froth is caused by a high concentration of detergents (which are generally basic/alkaline substances), the pH of the river water is most likely to be in the range:
subquestions.explanation: Detergents are generally alkaline (basic), so water heavily contaminated with them would have a pH noticeably above 7, in the 10-11 range.

subquestions.question: Water with a high concentration of dissolved detergent (a base) would show:
options: a high concentration of hydroxide ions (OH-) and a low concentration of hydronium ions (H3O+)
a low concentration of hydroxide ions (OH-) and a high concentration of hydronium ions (H3O+)
high concentrations of both OH- and H3O+
equal concentrations of OH- and H3O+
subquestions.explanation: A basic (alkaline) solution has a higher concentration of hydroxide ions (OH-) than hydronium ions (H3O+).

subquestions.question: High phosphate content in the river (from detergents) is found to decrease the dissolved oxygen level and increase algae growth. Explain briefly why this happens, and suggest a way to neutralise a sample of the contaminated (basic) water.

rubric.point: Phosphates act as a nutrient, causing excessive algae growth (eutrophication); as algae die and decompose, oxygen is consumed, lowering dissolved oxygen levels
To neutralise the basic water, treat it with a mild acid such as vinegar (dilute acetic acid)

subquestions.model_answer: The excess phosphate acts as a nutrient that causes rapid, excessive growth of algae (eutrophication). As this algae eventually dies and is decomposed by bacteria, the decomposition process consumes large amounts of dissolved oxygen, leaving too little for fish and other aquatic life to survive. Since the contaminated water is basic (alkaline), it can be neutralised by treating it with a mild acid, such as vinegar (dilute acetic acid).

questions.question: Neetu has two unlabeled test tubes containing dilute hydrochloric acid and dilute sodium hydroxide solution. Adding which of the following will help her visually identify the acidic and basic solution?
questions.explanation: Baking soda (sodium hydrogen carbonate) reacts with an acid to produce visible effervescence (CO2 gas bubbles), but shows no visible reaction with a base - so adding it to both test tubes will let her identify which one is the acid (the one that fizzes).

notes.overview: This chapter compares the physical and chemical properties that distinguish metals from non-metals, explains how metals react with oxygen, water and acids, introduces the reactivity series and its use in predicting displacement reactions, describes ionic bond formation, outlines how metals are extracted from their ores based on their reactivity, and covers corrosion and its prevention.

sections.title: 1. Physical Properties of Metals and Non-metals
sections.content: Metals are generally malleable (can be hammered into thin sheets), ductile (can be drawn into wires), good conductors of heat and electricity, lustrous (shiny), sonorous (produce a ringing sound when struck), and have high melting and boiling points (with exceptions like mercury, which is liquid at room temperature, and sodium/potassium, which are soft and have low melting points). Non-metals are generally brittle (break when hammered), poor conductors of heat and electricity (except graphite, a form of carbon), and lack lustre (except iodine); they may exist as solids, liquids (bromine) or gases at room temperature.
sections.video_title: Difference Between Metals and Non-metals (Magnet Brains)

sections.title: 2. Reaction of Metals with Oxygen
sections.content: Most metals react with oxygen to form metal oxides, which are generally basic in nature (turn red litmus blue if soluble, e.g. Na2O, MgO), while non-metal oxides are generally acidic (turn blue litmus red, e.g. CO2, SO2). Metals like potassium and sodium react so vigorously with oxygen at room temperature that they are stored in kerosene oil to prevent accidental fires; metals like aluminium form a thin protective oxide layer (Al2O3) on their surface that prevents further reaction, a property exploited in anodising.

sections.title: 3. Reaction of Metals with Water and Acids
sections.content: Highly reactive metals like sodium and potassium react vigorously with cold water, producing metal hydroxide and hydrogen gas (with the reaction being exothermic enough to catch fire); metals like magnesium and calcium react with cold water more slowly, while metals like iron react only with steam. Metals above hydrogen in the reactivity series react with dilute acids to liberate hydrogen gas and form a salt (e.g. Zn + 2HCl -> ZnCl2 + H2), while metals below hydrogen, like copper, do not react with dilute acids in this way.
keywords: sodium potassium react vigorously with water
metals react with acids liberate hydrogen

sections.title: 4. The Reactivity Series and Displacement Reactions
sections.content: The reactivity series arranges metals in decreasing order of their reactivity: Potassium, Sodium, Calcium, Magnesium, Aluminium, Zinc, Iron, Lead, (Hydrogen), Copper, Silver, Gold. A more reactive metal can displace a less reactive metal from its salt solution (a displacement reaction), for example iron displacing copper from copper sulphate solution (Fe + CuSO4 -> FeSO4 + Cu), while a less reactive metal cannot displace a more reactive one.

sections.title: 5. Formation of Ionic Compounds
sections.content: Ionic (electrovalent) compounds form when a metal atom transfers one or more electrons to a non-metal atom: the metal atom loses electrons to form a positively charged cation, achieving a stable electronic configuration, while the non-metal atom gains those electrons to form a negatively charged anion, also achieving stability; the oppositely charged ions are then held together by strong electrostatic forces of attraction, forming an ionic bond, e.g. in sodium chloride, sodium loses one electron to form Na+, and chlorine gains one electron to form Cl-.
sections.video_title: Reaction Between Metals and Non-Metals - Ionic Bond Formation (Magnet Brains)

sections.title: 6. Properties of Ionic Compounds
sections.content: Ionic compounds are generally solids with high melting and boiling points, due to the strong forces of attraction between their oppositely charged ions; they are generally soluble in water and insoluble in solvents like kerosene; and while solid ionic compounds do not conduct electricity (since ions are held in fixed positions), they do conduct electricity when molten or dissolved in water, because the ions then become free to move and carry charge.
sections.video_title: Reaction Between Metals and Non-Metals - Ionic Bond Formation (Magnet Brains)

sections.title: 7. Extraction of Metals
sections.content: Metals occur in nature as free elements (highly unreactive metals like gold and silver) or combined in ores as compounds (oxides, sulphides, carbonates); the extraction method used depends on the metal's position in the reactivity series. Highly reactive metals (like sodium, potassium, aluminium) are extracted by electrolytic reduction of their molten ores/compounds; moderately reactive metals (like zinc, iron, copper) are extracted by reducing their oxides with carbon (e.g. in a blast furnace) after first converting the ore to oxide form via roasting (sulphide ores) or calcination (carbonate ores); the extracted metal is then refined, commonly by electrolytic refining, to obtain a pure form.

sections.title: 8. Corrosion and its Prevention
sections.content: Corrosion is the gradual deterioration of a metal due to its reaction with substances in the surrounding environment (moisture, air, acids), such as the rusting of iron, in which iron reacts with oxygen and moisture in the air to form hydrated iron(III) oxide (rust). Corrosion can be prevented by methods such as painting, oiling/greasing, galvanisation (coating iron with a thin layer of zinc), electroplating (coating with a less reactive metal such as chromium), and alloying (mixing with other metals, e.g. converting iron into stainless steel, which resists rusting).

sections.title: 9. Alloys
sections.content: An alloy is a homogeneous mixture of two or more metals, or a metal and a non-metal, prepared by first melting the primary metal and then dissolving the other elements in it in a definite proportion, followed by cooling to room temperature; alloying generally changes the properties of the pure metal in a useful way - for example, alloying iron with carbon and other metals produces stainless steel, which resists rusting, and alloying copper with tin produces bronze, which is harder and more durable than pure copper.

key_terms.Malleability: The property of a metal that allows it to be hammered or beaten into thin sheets without breaking.
key_terms.Ductility: The property of a metal that allows it to be drawn into thin wires.
key_terms.Reactivity series: A list of metals arranged in decreasing order of their chemical reactivity.
key_terms.Displacement reaction: A reaction in which a more reactive metal displaces a less reactive metal from its salt solution.
key_terms.Corrosion: The gradual deterioration of a metal due to reaction with substances in its environment, such as rusting.
key_terms.Alloy: A homogeneous mixture of two or more metals, or a metal and a non-metal, with modified useful properties.

important_facts: Metal oxides are generally basic; non-metal oxides are generally acidic.
Sodium and potassium are stored in kerosene oil because they react vigorously with air and water.
Reactivity series (decreasing order): K, Na, Ca, Mg, Al, Zn, Fe, Pb, (H), Cu, Ag, Au.
Rusting of iron requires both oxygen and moisture; it is prevented by galvanisation, painting, oiling, or alloying.
Ionic compounds conduct electricity only in the molten state or when dissolved in water, not as solids.
exam_tips: Be ready to write balanced equations for displacement reactions and reactions of metals with dilute acids - a very common source of questions.
Learn the reactivity series order thoroughly, since many questions ask you to predict whether a reaction will occur.
Distinguish clearly between roasting (used for sulphide ores) and calcination (used for carbonate ores) when explaining extraction of metals.

questions.model_answer: Metals and non-metals differ in several physical properties. First, metals are malleable and ductile - for example, gold can be beaten into thin sheets and copper can be drawn into wires - whereas non-metals like sulphur are brittle and break when hammered. Second, metals like copper and silver are excellent conductors of heat and electricity, while most non-metals (except graphite) are poor conductors. questions.model_answer: Ionic compounds have high melting points because the oppositely charged ions in their crystal lattice are held together by strong electrostatic forces of attraction, which require a large amount of energy to overcome. They are generally soluble in water because polar water molecules can surround the individual ions and pull them away from the lattice, effectively dissolving the compound. They conduct electricity only when molten or dissolved in water because only then are the ions free to move and carry electric charge; in the solid state, the ions are held rigidly in fixed positions within the lattice and cannot move, so no current flows.

questions.question: Explain how the method used to extract a metal from its ore depends on its position in the reactivity series, giving one example for each category.

Moderately reactive metals (middle of series, e.g. zinc, iron): extracted by reducing their oxides with carbon
Metals low in reactivity (e.g. gold, silver): found in free/native state and require little to no extraction chemistry

questions.model_answer: The extraction method for a metal depends on its position in the reactivity series. Highly reactive metals near the top of the series, such as sodium and aluminium, cannot be reduced by carbon and are instead extracted by electrolytic reduction of their molten oxides or salts. Moderately reactive metals in the middle of the series, such as zinc and iron, can be extracted by reducing their oxides with carbon (as in a blast furnace for iron). Metals with very low reactivity, such as gold and silver, occur in nature in their free (native) state and require comparatively little chemical processing to obtain the pure metal.

questions.model_answer: Corrosion is the gradual deterioration of a metal due to its reaction with substances present in its surrounding environment, such as air, moisture, or acids. In the case of iron, this process is called rusting: iron reacts with oxygen and moisture in the air over time to form hydrated iron(III) oxide, a reddish-brown, flaky substance that weakens the metal. Rusting can be prevented by galvanisation, in which a thin protective layer of zinc is coated onto the iron's surface; this zinc layer physically shields the underlying iron from exposure to air and moisture, and even if scratched, the zinc corrodes preferentially, continuing to protect the iron beneath.

questions.model_answer: Non-metal oxides are generally acidic because they react with water to form an acid. For example, carbon dioxide dissolves in water to form carbonic acid: CO2 + H2O -> H2CO3. Reaction with oxygen: metals form basic oxides (some amphoteric, e.g. Al2O3, ZnO); non-metals form acidic oxides
Reaction with water: reactive metals like sodium/potassium react vigorously with cold water; less reactive metals react with steam or not at all; non-metals generally do not react with water

rubric.point: Reaction with acids: metals above hydrogen in the reactivity series liberate hydrogen gas with dilute acids; non-metals generally do not react with dilute acids in this way

rubric.point: Oxide nature: metal oxides are basic (turn red litmus blue, if soluble); non-metal oxides are acidic (turn blue litmus red)

questions.model_answer: (a) Physical properties: Metals are generally malleable (can be hammered into sheets), ductile (can be drawn into wires), lustrous, sonorous, and good conductors of heat and electricity. Non-metals are generally brittle, lack lustre, and are poor conductors of heat and electricity, with graphite being a notable exception. (b) Reaction with oxygen: Metals react with oxygen to form metal oxides, which are generally basic in nature (some, like aluminium oxide and zinc oxide, are amphoteric). Non-metals react with oxygen to form non-metal oxides, which are generally acidic in nature. (c) Reaction with water: Highly reactive metals like sodium and potassium react vigorously with cold water, less reactive metals like magnesium react slowly or only with steam (like iron), while unreactive metals like copper and gold do not react with water at all. Non-metals generally do not react with water. (d) Reaction with acids: Metals placed above hydrogen in the reactivity series react with dilute acids to liberate hydrogen gas and form a salt, while metals below hydrogen, like copper, do not. Non-metals generally do not react with dilute acids to liberate hydrogen. (e) Oxide nature: Metal oxides are basic in nature (soluble ones turn red litmus blue), while non-metal oxides are acidic in nature (they turn blue litmus red).

questions.question: Describe the general steps involved in the extraction of a moderately reactive metal (such as iron or zinc) from its ore, from mining to obtaining the pure metal.

rubric.point: Ores are first crushed and concentrated (enrichment) to remove impurities like sand and rocky material
Sulphide ores are converted to oxides via roasting (heating in excess air); carbonate ores are converted via calcination (heating in limited air)
The metal oxide is then reduced to the free metal, commonly using carbon (coke) as a reducing agent, e.g. in a blast furnace for iron
The extracted metal, usually impure, is then refined - commonly by electrolytic refining, in which impure metal is made the anode and pure metal deposits at the cathode
The overall sequence depends on the metal's reactivity, since more reactive metals require electrolytic reduction rather than reduction with carbon
keywords: electrolytic reduction for very reactive metals

questions.model_answer: Extraction of a moderately reactive metal from its ore typically follows several steps. First, the ore is mined and then crushed and concentrated (enriched) to remove unwanted impurities such as sand and rocky material. Next, the concentrated ore is converted into the metal oxide: sulphide ores are converted via roasting (heating strongly in the presence of excess air), while carbonate ores are converted via calcination (heating strongly with limited air, releasing carbon dioxide). The resulting metal oxide is then reduced to the free metal - commonly by heating it with carbon (coke) as a reducing agent, such as in a blast furnace used for extracting iron from iron oxide. Finally, the extracted metal, which is usually impure, is refined to obtain a purer form, most commonly through electrolytic refining, in which the impure metal is made the anode, a thin sheet of pure metal is made the cathode, and pure metal deposits at the cathode as electrolysis proceeds. This overall process depends on the metal's reactivity - more reactive metals like sodium or aluminium instead require electrolytic reduction of their molten compounds rather than reduction with carbon.

questions.model_answer: An alloy is a homogeneous mixture of two or more metals, or a metal and a non-metal, blended together usually by melting and mixing. Alloys are often preferred over pure metals because they typically have improved properties, such as greater strength, hardness, or resistance to corrosion, compared to the pure metal alone. For example, stainless steel (an alloy of iron, chromium and nickel) resists rusting much better than pure iron, making it more suitable for use in cutlery and kitchen equipment.

questions.question: (a) Explain how an ionic compound like sodium chloride (NaCl) is formed, showing the transfer of electrons. (b) State three general properties of ionic compounds and briefly explain why each occurs.

rubric.point: (a) Sodium (2,8,1) loses one electron to form Na+ (stable octet); chlorine (2,8,7) gains that electron to form Cl- (stable octet)
(a) Oppositely charged Na+ and Cl- ions attract each other, forming an ionic bond
(b) Three properties with reasons, e.g. high melting/boiling point (strong electrostatic forces), conduct electricity in molten/aqueous state (free-moving ions), soluble in water (polar solvent)

questions.model_answer: (a) Sodium has the electronic configuration 2,8,1 and loses its single outermost electron to achieve a stable octet, forming a positively charged Na+ ion. Chlorine has the configuration 2,8,7 and gains that electron to complete its own octet, forming a negatively charged Cl- ion. The oppositely charged Na+ and Cl- ions are then held together by strong electrostatic forces of attraction, forming the ionic bond in sodium chloride. (b) Three properties of ionic compounds: (1) They have high melting and boiling points, because a large amount of energy is needed to overcome the strong electrostatic forces holding the ions together in the crystal lattice. (2) They conduct electricity when molten or dissolved in water, because the ions become free to move and carry charge (but not in the solid state, where ions are fixed in place). (3) They are generally soluble in water, since water is a polar solvent that can surround and separate the charged ions.

questions.question:
Galvanisation coats iron articles with a layer of zinc to prevent rusting. The iron stays protected even if the zinc coating is scratched and the iron underneath is exposed. Which statement(s) explain why zinc protects the iron?
P) A galvanised iron article does not undergo oxidation.
Q) The zinc coating prevents contact of iron with air.
R) Zinc undergoes corrosion more easily than iron.
questions.explanation: The zinc coating normally protects iron by physically keeping air/moisture off it (Q). But even where the coating is scratched, iron stays protected because zinc is more reactive than iron and corrodes preferentially, sacrificially protecting the iron underneath (R) - this is why P (that the article never oxidises at all) is not correct.

Assertion (A): Zinc oxide can be reduced to zinc metal on heating with carbon.
Reason (R): Carbon is less reactive than zinc.

Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.

A is false but R is true.

Reason (R): In electrorefining, metal ions accept electrons at the anode and are deposited as pure metal.

Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.

questions.topic: Comparing corrosion rates of iron and aluminium
questions.question: Equal-sized bars of aluminium and iron are exposed to the same environment, each marked with a line partway up. Which bar is likely to corrode up to the marked line first? Justify your answer by explaining what happens to each metal on exposure to air and moisture.

rubric.point: The iron bar corrodes to the marked line first

Iron reacts with oxygen and moisture to form a loose, flaky layer of rust (hydrated iron oxide) that does not adhere firmly, so air and moisture keep reaching the metal beneath and corrosion continues progressively

Aluminium forms a thin, tightly-adhering layer of aluminium oxide on exposure to air, and this protective oxide layer prevents further oxygen/moisture from reaching the metal underneath, so corrosion effectively stops

questions.model_answer: The iron bar will corrode up to the marked line first. Iron reacts with the oxygen and moisture in air to form rust (hydrated iron(III) oxide), which forms a loose, porous, flaking layer that does not protect the metal underneath - so air and moisture keep reaching fresh iron and corrosion continues to eat into the bar. Aluminium, in contrast, reacts with atmospheric oxygen to form a thin but tightly-adhering layer of aluminium oxide on its surface; this layer acts as a protective coating that seals off the metal beneath from further contact with air and moisture, so once it forms, further corrosion is effectively stopped.

questions.topic: Ionic bond formation from electronic configuration
questions.question: The electronic configurations of six elements are: P(2,8,8), Q(2,8,8,1), R(2,6), S(2,5), T(2,8,2), U(2,8,7). (a) Identify any two pairs of these elements that would react to form an ionic compound by transfer of electrons. (b) Write the molecular formula of the compound formed by each pair.

rubric.point: Elements with 1-2 electrons in the outermost shell (Q, has 1 valence electron; T, has 2 valence electrons) readily lose electrons to form cations, while elements with 6-7 valence electrons (R has 6, U has 7) readily gain electrons to form anions - so valid reacting pairs include Q+U, Q+R, T+R, or T+U
For a pair like Q (1 valence electron, forms +1 ion) and U (7 valence electrons, forms -1 ion), the compound formula is QU (1:1 ratio)

For a pair like T (2 valence electrons, forms +2 ion) and R (6 valence electrons, forms -2 ion), the compound formula is TR (1:1, since charges balance); for T with U (-1 ion), the formula would be TU2

questions.model_answer: Q (2,8,8,1) has 1 valence electron and readily loses it to form a +1 ion; T (2,8,2) has 2 valence electrons and readily loses them to form a +2 ion. R (2,6) has 6 valence electrons and readily gains 2 to form a -2 ion; U (2,8,7) has 7 valence electrons and readily gains 1 to form a -1 ion. Two valid ionic pairs are Q and U, forming QU (charges +1 and -1 balance in a 1:1 ratio), and T and R, forming TR (charges +2 and -2 balance in a 1:1 ratio). (T and U would instead give TU2, since one T2+ needs two U- ions to balance charge.)

questions.topic: Reactivity series - carbon reduction and electrolytic reduction of very reactive metals
questions.question: (a) Explain why carbon cannot be used to reduce the oxides of sodium, magnesium, calcium and aluminium to their respective metals. (b) These metals are instead obtained by electrolytic reduction of their molten chlorides. Write the reactions occurring at the anode and cathode during the electrolytic reduction of molten sodium chloride. (c) With the help of a chemical equation, illustrate the reduction of manganese dioxide using aluminium powder.

rubric.point: Sodium, magnesium, calcium and aluminium are more reactive than carbon (they have a greater affinity for oxygen than carbon does), so carbon cannot displace/reduce them from their oxides
Electrolysis of molten NaCl: at the cathode, Na+ + e- -> Na; at the anode, 2Cl- -> Cl2 + 2e-
Thermite-type reaction: 3MnO2 + 4Al -> 3Mn + 2Al2O3 + heat

questions.model_answer: Sodium, magnesium, calcium and aluminium are all more reactive than carbon - they have a stronger affinity for oxygen than carbon does - so carbon cannot displace them from their oxides by reduction; instead they are extracted by electrolytic reduction of their molten salts. For molten sodium chloride: at the cathode, sodium ions gain electrons and are reduced, Na+ + e- -> Na; at the anode, chloride ions lose electrons and are oxidised to chlorine gas, 2Cl- -> Cl2 + 2e-. Manganese dioxide can be reduced using aluminium powder (a thermite-type reaction): 3MnO2(s) + 4Al(s) -> 3Mn(l) + 2Al2O3(s) + heat.

subquestions.model_answer: In electrolytic refining, the impure copper is made the anode, and a strip of pure copper is used as the cathode, with an acidified aqueous solution of copper sulphate (CuSO4) as the electrolyte. When current is passed, copper from the impure anode dissolves into the electrolyte as Cu2+ ions, which then get deposited as pure copper onto the cathode - so pure copper collects at the cathode, while heavier insoluble impurities settle at the bottom below the anode as 'anode mud'.
