notes.overview: This chapter explores why carbon forms such an enormous variety of compounds through covalent bonding and catenation, introduces saturated and unsaturated hydrocarbons and their nomenclature, describes common functional groups, and covers the chemical properties of carbon compounds - including combustion, oxidation, addition and substitution reactions - along with a focus on ethanol, ethanoic acid, and soaps and detergents.

sections.title: 1. Covalent Bonding in Carbon Compounds
sections.content: Carbon has 4 electrons in its outermost shell; rather than gaining or losing 4 electrons (which would require too much energy), carbon atoms achieve a stable electronic configuration by sharing electrons with other atoms (of carbon or other elements like hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, chlorine), forming covalent bonds. A single covalent bond involves the sharing of one electron pair, a double bond involves two electron pairs, and a triple bond involves three electron pairs, between two atoms.

sections.title: 2. Versatile Nature of Carbon - Catenation
sections.content: Carbon has a unique property called catenation - the ability to form covalent bonds with other carbon atoms, creating long straight chains, branched chains, or rings of carbon atoms - a property shown to a much smaller extent by very few other elements (like silicon). Combined with carbon's ability to form strong bonds with hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, sulphur and various other elements, catenation explains why carbon forms such a vast number of compounds, far exceeding the compounds of all other elements combined.

sections.title: 3. Saturated and Unsaturated Hydrocarbons
sections.content: Hydrocarbons are compounds made up of only carbon and hydrogen. Saturated hydrocarbons (alkanes, general formula CnH2n+2) contain only single covalent bonds between carbon atoms, e.g. methane (CH4), ethane (C2H6). Unsaturated hydrocarbons contain at least one double bond (alkenes, general formula CnH2n, e.g. ethene C2H4) or triple bond (alkynes, general formula CnH2n-2, e.g. ethyne C2H2) between carbon atoms, and are generally more reactive than saturated hydrocarbons.
keywords: unsaturated alkenes alkynes double triple bonds

sections.title: 4. Functional Groups and Homologous Series
sections.content: A functional group is a specific atom or group of atoms attached to a carbon chain that determines the characteristic chemical properties of the compound, e.g. -OH (alcohol), -CHO (aldehyde), -COOH (carboxylic acid), -X (halogen, where X = Cl, Br, I). A homologous series is a family of compounds having the same functional group and general formula, in which each successive member differs from the previous one by a -CH2- unit, and members show a gradual change in physical properties (like melting/boiling point) but similar chemical properties.

sections.title: 5. Nomenclature of Carbon Compounds
sections.content: Naming a carbon compound generally involves identifying the number of carbon atoms in the longest chain (using prefixes like meth-, eth-, prop-, but-, for 1, 2, 3, 4 carbons), and modifying the name based on the functional group present - e.g. replacing the final '-e' with '-ol' for an alcohol (ethane -> ethanol), with '-al' for an aldehyde, with '-oic acid' for a carboxylic acid (ethane -> ethanoic acid), and using 'di', 'tri' etc. for multiple double bonds or substituents as needed.
sections.video_title: IUPAC Nomenclature of Carbon Compounds (Magnet Brains)

sections.title: 6. Chemical Properties - Combustion and Oxidation
sections.content: Carbon compounds, especially hydrocarbons, burn in air/oxygen (combustion) to produce carbon dioxide, water, and heat/light energy, e.g. CH4 + 2O2 -> CO2 + 2H2O; saturated hydrocarbons generally burn with a clean blue flame, while unsaturated hydrocarbons burn with a more yellow, sooty flame due to incomplete combustion. Alcohols can be oxidised to carboxylic acids using oxidising agents like alkaline potassium permanganate (KMnO4) or acidified potassium dichromate, e.g. ethanol is oxidised to ethanoic acid.
keywords: saturated clean flame unsaturated sooty flame
sections.video_title: Why do Substances Burn With or Without a Flame? - Combustion (Magnet Brains)

sections.title: 7. Chemical Properties - Addition and Substitution Reactions
sections.content: Addition reactions occur in unsaturated hydrocarbons, where hydrogen is added across a double or triple bond in the presence of a catalyst like nickel, converting an unsaturated compound into a saturated one (hydrogenation), e.g. used in converting vegetable oils into vegetable ghee (solid fats). Substitution reactions occur in saturated hydrocarbons, typically in the presence of sunlight, where hydrogen atoms are progressively replaced by other atoms like chlorine, e.g. methane reacting with chlorine to form chloromethane and, eventually, more highly substituted products.

sections.title: 8. Ethanol and Ethanoic Acid
sections.content: Ethanol (C2H5OH), commonly known as alcohol, is a liquid that is completely miscible with water, reacts with sodium metal to liberate hydrogen gas, and is used as a solvent and in the preparation of medicines and beverages, though excessive consumption impairs the body and is harmful to health. Ethanoic acid (CH3COOH), commonly known as acetic acid (present as about 5-8% in vinegar), is a weak acid that turns blue litmus red, reacts with sodium hydrogen carbonate to liberate carbon dioxide gas (a characteristic identification test), and reacts with alcohols in the presence of an acid catalyst to form a sweet-smelling ester.
keywords: ethanoic acid vinegar reacts with sodium hydrogen carbonate

sections.title: 9. Soaps and Detergents
sections.content: Soaps are sodium or potassium salts of long-chain fatty acids, having a molecule with two distinct parts: a hydrophilic (water-loving) ionic 'head' and a hydrophobic (water-repelling) hydrocarbon 'tail'; in water, soap molecules cluster together around grease/oil droplets to form structures called micelles, with tails pointing inward (into the oil/grease) and heads pointing outward (into water), allowing the oil/grease to be suspended in water and washed away. Unlike soaps, synthetic detergents remain effective even in hard water (which contains calcium and magnesium ions that react with soap to form an insoluble scum), since detergents do not form such a precipitate with these ions.

key_terms.Covalent bond: A chemical bond formed by the sharing of a pair of electrons between two atoms.
key_terms.Catenation: The unique ability of carbon atoms to form covalent bonds with other carbon atoms, forming chains, branches or rings.
key_terms.Functional group: An atom or group of atoms attached to a carbon chain that determines the compound's characteristic chemical properties.
key_terms.Homologous series: A family of compounds with the same functional group, general formula, and similar chemical properties, differing by a -CH2- unit between successive members.
key_terms.Micelle: A cluster of soap molecules formed in water around oil/grease droplets, with hydrophobic tails inward and hydrophilic heads outward.
key_terms.Esterification: The reaction between an alcohol and a carboxylic acid (with an acid catalyst) to form a sweet-smelling ester.

important_facts: Carbon's tetravalency and catenation together explain the huge diversity of carbon compounds.
Saturated hydrocarbons (alkanes) contain only single bonds; unsaturated hydrocarbons (alkenes, alkynes) contain double or triple bonds.
Ethanoic acid reacting with sodium hydrogen carbonate to release CO2 gas (with brisk effervescence) is a standard test/identification reaction.
Soap molecules form micelles in water, trapping grease/oil at the centre so it can be washed away.
Detergents work in hard water because, unlike soap, they do not form an insoluble scum with calcium/magnesium ions.
exam_tips: Practice drawing electron dot (Lewis) structures for simple covalent molecules like methane, ethane, ethene, and ethyne - a common question type.
Be ready to write and balance the combustion equation for common hydrocarbons, and to distinguish complete (blue flame) from incomplete (yellow, sooty flame) combustion.
Remember the key test for ethanoic acid: brisk effervescence (CO2 gas) with sodium hydrogen carbonate - a frequently asked practical-based question.

questions.question: What is catenation? Why does carbon form a far greater number of compounds through catenation than silicon, the only other element showing this property to a notable extent?

rubric.point: Catenation is the ability of an atom to form bonds with atoms of the same element, creating chains, branches or rings
Carbon-carbon bonds are much stronger than silicon-silicon bonds, so carbon can form long, stable chains, while silicon's self-bonds are comparatively weak and limited

questions.model_answer: Catenation is the property by which atoms of an element can form covalent bonds with other atoms of the same element, creating long chains, branched chains, or rings. Carbon shows this property to an extraordinary extent because carbon-carbon bonds are exceptionally strong and stable, allowing very long and complex chains to form. Silicon, the only other element showing catenation to a notable degree, forms much weaker silicon-silicon bonds, so its ability to form long chains is far more limited than carbon's, resulting in carbon forming a vastly greater number and variety of compounds.

questions.question: Write the equation for the reaction between ethanol and ethanoic acid (esterification), and state one property of the product formed.

rubric.point: Equation: C2H5OH + CH3COOH -> CH3COOC2H5 + H2O (in the presence of concentrated sulphuric acid as catalyst)
The ester formed has a sweet, fruity smell and is used in perfumes/flavourings

questions.model_answer: C2H5OH + CH3COOH -(conc. H2SO4)-> CH3COOC2H5 + H2O. The ester formed (ethyl ethanoate) has a characteristic sweet, fruity smell, quite different from the pungent smell of ethanoic acid, and such esters are widely used in making perfumes and as flavouring agents.

questions.question: Explain why carbon forms such an enormous number of compounds, referring to both catenation and tetravalency.

rubric.point: Tetravalency: carbon has 4 valence electrons, so it can form 4 covalent bonds, allowing it to bond with many different atoms/groups simultaneously
Catenation: carbon atoms can bond with each other to form long chains, branched chains, or rings, to an extent unmatched by other elements
Together, these allow an enormous variety of structural arrangements and combinations with other elements (H, O, N, halogens), producing a vast number of distinct compounds

questions.model_answer: Carbon forms an enormous number of compounds due to two combined properties. First, its tetravalency - having 4 electrons in its outermost shell - allows each carbon atom to form 4 covalent bonds, letting it link simultaneously with several different atoms or groups. Second, and most importantly, carbon shows a unique property called catenation: the ability to form strong, stable covalent bonds with other carbon atoms, creating long straight chains, branched chains, and rings, to an extent that no other element (except silicon, to a much smaller degree) can match. Together, tetravalency and catenation allow carbon to form an almost limitless variety of structural arrangements, further multiplied by combining with elements like hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen and halogens - resulting in millions of known carbon compounds, far outnumbering the compounds of all other elements combined.

questions.question: State three properties of ethanol and one important use, and mention one harmful effect of its consumption.

It reacts with sodium metal to liberate hydrogen gas
Used as a solvent/in medicines; consuming it in excess is harmful/impairs bodily functions

questions.model_answer: Ethanol is a colourless liquid that is completely miscible with water in all proportions. It reacts with sodium metal to liberate hydrogen gas: 2Na + 2C2H5OH -> 2C2H5ONa + H2. It is widely used as a solvent in the preparation of medicines, tinctures, and various industrial applications. However, when consumed as a beverage, especially in excess, ethanol impairs the functioning of the nervous system and can seriously harm the liver and other organs over time.

questions.question: Distinguish between an addition reaction and a substitution reaction in carbon compounds, giving one example of each with equations.

rubric.point: Addition reaction: occurs in unsaturated hydrocarbons; hydrogen (or another atom) adds across a double/triple bond, e.g. hydrogenation of ethene with a nickel catalyst: CH2=CH2 + H2 -(Ni)-> CH3-CH3
Substitution reaction: occurs in saturated hydrocarbons; an atom (commonly H) is replaced by another atom (like chlorine), typically requiring sunlight, e.g. CH4 + Cl2 -(sunlight)-> CH3Cl + HCl
Key distinction: addition adds atoms across a multiple bond (no atoms removed); substitution replaces an existing atom with a new one

questions.model_answer: An addition reaction occurs in unsaturated hydrocarbons, where an atom (commonly hydrogen) is added across a double or triple bond, converting the compound into a saturated one - for example, the hydrogenation of ethene using a nickel catalyst: CH2=CH2 + H2 -(Ni)-> CH3-CH3. A substitution reaction occurs in saturated hydrocarbons, where an existing atom (commonly hydrogen) is replaced by another atom, such as chlorine, typically in the presence of sunlight - for example, methane reacting with chlorine: CH4 + Cl2 -(sunlight)-> CH3Cl + HCl. The key distinction is that an addition reaction adds new atoms across a multiple bond without removing any existing atoms, whereas a substitution reaction replaces an atom already present in the molecule with a different one.

questions.topic: Soap vs detergent in hard water
questions.question: Explain why soap does not lather well in hard water, but detergents do, using appropriate chemical reasoning.

rubric.point: Hard water contains dissolved calcium and magnesium salts/ions
Soap reacts with these calcium/magnesium ions to form an insoluble scum (precipitate), which reduces lathering and wastes soap
keywords: soap forms insoluble scum with calcium magnesium

rubric.point: Detergents, unlike soap, do not form such an insoluble precipitate with calcium/magnesium ions, so they continue to lather effectively even in hard water

questions.model_answer: Hard water contains dissolved calcium and magnesium salts. When soap is used in hard water, it reacts with these calcium and magnesium ions to form an insoluble scum (a precipitate), which is wasted soap and also reduces the amount of lather produced, making cleaning less effective. Synthetic detergents, however, are specifically designed so that they do not form an insoluble precipitate with calcium and magnesium ions; as a result, they continue to lather effectively and clean well even in hard water, unlike ordinary soap.

questions.question: What is a homologous series? Describe two characteristics of members of a homologous series, using the alkane series as an example.

rubric.point: A homologous series is a family of compounds with the same functional group and general formula, where successive members differ by a -CH2- unit
Members show a gradual, regular change in physical properties (like melting/boiling point) as molecular size increases
Members show similar chemical properties, since they share the same functional group (e.g. all alkanes undergo similar substitution/combustion reactions)

questions.model_answer: A homologous series is a family of organic compounds having the same functional group and the same general formula, in which each successive member differs from the one before it by a fixed -CH2- unit. For example, the alkane series - methane (CH4), ethane (C2H6), propane (C3H8), and so on - shows two key characteristics: first, physical properties like melting point and boiling point change gradually and regularly as the chain length (molecular mass) increases; second, all members show similar chemical properties, since they share the same type of bonding and functional characteristics - for instance, all alkanes undergo similar combustion and substitution reactions.

questions.topic: Ethanol and ethanoic acid - comprehensive comparison
questions.question: Compare ethanol and ethanoic acid under the headings: (a) functional group and general nature, (b) reaction with sodium metal, (c) reaction with sodium hydrogen carbonate, (d) common uses, and (e) one distinguishing chemical test.

rubric.point: Functional group: ethanol has -OH (alcohol); ethanoic acid has -COOH (carboxylic acid, weak acid)
Reaction with sodium: both liberate hydrogen gas (2Na + 2C2H5OH -> 2C2H5ONa + H2; 2Na + 2CH3COOH -> 2CH3COONa + H2)
keywords: both react with sodium liberate hydrogen

rubric.point: Reaction with sodium hydrogen carbonate: ethanoic acid reacts with brisk effervescence releasing CO2; ethanol does not react
keywords: ethanoic acid reacts with NaHCO3 CO2

rubric.point: Uses: ethanol used as solvent/in medicines/beverages; ethanoic acid used as vinegar (food preservative/flavouring)
Distinguishing test: sodium hydrogen carbonate test - ethanoic acid gives brisk effervescence (CO2), ethanol shows no such reaction, distinguishing the two

questions.model_answer: (a) Functional group and nature: Ethanol contains the -OH (hydroxyl) functional group, characteristic of alcohols, and is a neutral compound. Ethanoic acid contains the -COOH (carboxyl) functional group, characteristic of carboxylic acids, and behaves as a weak acid. (b) Reaction with sodium: Both react with sodium metal to liberate hydrogen gas - ethanol: 2Na + 2C2H5OH -> 2C2H5ONa + H2; ethanoic acid: 2Na + 2CH3COOH -> 2CH3COONa + H2. (c) Reaction with sodium hydrogen carbonate: Ethanoic acid reacts vigorously with sodium hydrogen carbonate, producing brisk effervescence due to carbon dioxide gas (CH3COOH + NaHCO3 -> CH3COONa + H2O + CO2), while ethanol does not react with sodium hydrogen carbonate at all. (d) Uses: Ethanol is widely used as a solvent, in the preparation of medicines and tinctures, and (in regulated form) in beverages, though excess consumption is harmful. Ethanoic acid, present as 5-8% in vinegar, is used as a food preservative and flavouring agent, and industrially in making various chemicals. (e) Distinguishing test: The sodium hydrogen carbonate test clearly distinguishes the two - ethanoic acid produces brisk effervescence (CO2 gas), while ethanol shows no visible reaction, making this a simple and reliable way to tell the two compounds apart.

questions.question: What is esterification? Write the general reaction and state one use of esters.

rubric.point: Esterification is the reaction of a carboxylic acid with an alcohol (usually with an acid catalyst) to form an ester and water
General reaction: acid + alcohol -> ester + water
Use of esters, e.g. used in making perfumes/flavouring agents due to their pleasant, fruity smell

questions.model_answer: Esterification is the chemical reaction between a carboxylic acid and an alcohol, usually in the presence of a small amount of concentrated sulphuric acid as a catalyst, to form an ester along with water. The general reaction is: carboxylic acid + alcohol -> ester + water. Esters have a pleasant, fruity smell, so they are widely used in making perfumes and as artificial flavouring agents in the food industry.

questions.question: What is saponification? Name the raw materials typically used, and the products formed.

rubric.point: Saponification is the reaction in which a fat/oil is hydrolysed by an alkali (like NaOH) to form soap
Raw materials: vegetable oils or animal fats, plus a strong alkali such as sodium hydroxide (NaOH)
Products: soap (sodium salt of a fatty acid) and glycerol

questions.model_answer: Saponification is the chemical process in which a fat or oil is hydrolysed by heating it with a strong alkali, forming soap. The raw materials typically used are vegetable oils or animal fats, along with a strong alkali such as sodium hydroxide (NaOH). This reaction produces soap (the sodium salt of a long-chain fatty acid) along with glycerol as a by-product.

questions.topic: Comprehensive - catenation and covalent bonding in carbon
questions.question: (a) What is catenation, and why is carbon especially good at it compared to other elements? (b) Explain why carbon forms covalent compounds rather than ionic compounds. (c) Give one example each of a straight-chain, branched-chain, and cyclic carbon compound.

rubric.point: (a) Catenation is the ability of an atom to form bonds with other atoms of the same element, forming long chains/rings
(a) Carbon forms strong C-C bonds and can bond with up to 4 other atoms, giving it an exceptional ability to catenate compared to most other elements
(b) Carbon has 4 valence electrons; gaining or losing 4 electrons would require too much energy, so it shares electrons (forms covalent bonds) instead
(c) Give valid examples: straight-chain (e.g. butane), branched-chain (e.g. isobutane), cyclic (e.g. cyclohexane/benzene)

questions.model_answer: (a) Catenation is the unique ability of an atom to form bonds with other atoms of the same element, creating long chains, branched structures, or rings. Carbon is exceptionally good at catenation because it forms strong, stable carbon-carbon (C-C) bonds and is tetravalent (can form 4 bonds), allowing it to link with many other carbon atoms while still bonding with other elements too. (b) Carbon has 4 electrons in its outermost shell. Gaining 4 electrons or losing 4 electrons to achieve a stable octet would require far too much energy, so instead carbon achieves stability by sharing its electrons with other atoms, forming covalent bonds and covalent compounds rather than ionic ones. (c) Examples: a straight-chain compound is butane (CH3-CH2-CH2-CH3); a branched-chain compound is isobutane (2-methylpropane); a cyclic compound is cyclohexane (a six-carbon ring).

questions.topic: Comprehensive - homologous series and functional groups
questions.question: (a) What is a homologous series? State two characteristics of members of a homologous series. (b) Explain the role of a functional group with reference to the -OH group in alcohols. (c) Write the molecular formulas of the first three members of the alkane series.

rubric.point: (a) A homologous series is a series of compounds with the same general formula and similar chemical properties, differing by a -CH2- unit between successive members
(a) Two characteristics: successive members differ by CH2 (14 mass units), and all members show similar chemical properties due to the same functional group

(b) A functional group is a specific atom/group of atoms that determines the chemical properties of a compound; the -OH (hydroxyl) group makes a compound an alcohol and is responsible for its characteristic reactions
(c) CH4 (methane), C2H6 (ethane), C3H8 (propane)

questions.model_answer: (a) A homologous series is a series of organic compounds having the same general formula, in which each successive member differs from the one before it by a fixed unit of -CH2- (14 mass units). Two characteristics of members of a homologous series are: they show a gradual change in physical properties (like melting/boiling point) as molecular mass increases, and they show similar chemical properties, since they share the same functional group. (b) A functional group is a specific atom or group of atoms attached to a carbon chain that determines the characteristic chemical properties of a compound. In alcohols, the -OH (hydroxyl) group is the functional group; it is responsible for the characteristic reactions of alcohols, such as reacting with sodium metal to release hydrogen gas, regardless of how long the carbon chain is. (c) The first three members of the alkane series are: methane (CH4), ethane (C2H6), and propane (C3H8).

questions.topic: Case study - saturated vs unsaturated hydrocarbon structures
questions.passage: Below is described a four-carbon skeleton (four carbon atoms joined in a chain, C-C-C-C) of a hydrocarbon compound, to which hydrogen atoms are to be added to complete different possible molecules.

subquestions.question: Starting from a four-carbon chain skeleton, describe how you would add hydrogen atoms/bonds to form (i) a saturated hydrocarbon, and (ii) an unsaturated hydrocarbon, from this skeleton.

rubric.point: For a saturated hydrocarbon (an alkane, butane C4H10), every carbon-carbon bond is a single bond, and each carbon atom is bonded to as many hydrogen atoms as needed to complete its four bonds (giving CH3-CH2-CH2-CH3)
For an unsaturated hydrocarbon (an alkene or alkyne), at least one carbon-carbon bond is a double or triple bond, so fewer hydrogen atoms are attached overall (e.g. but-1-ene, CH2=CH-CH2-CH3, C4H8)

subquestions.model_answer: To form a saturated hydrocarbon from the four-carbon skeleton, every C-C bond is kept as a single bond and each carbon is given as many hydrogen atoms as needed to complete its four bonds, giving the alkane butane, CH3-CH2-CH2-CH3 (C4H10). To form an unsaturated hydrocarbon, one C-C bond is instead made a double or triple bond, which uses up two (or four) of the bonding positions that would otherwise go to hydrogen atoms - for example but-1-ene, CH2=CH-CH2-CH3 (C4H8), an alkene.

subquestions.question: If the four-carbon skeleton is that of a straight-chain alkene, draw/describe the structures of all the possible compounds.

But-2-ene: CH3-CH=CH-CH3 (double bond between C2 and C3)

subquestions.model_answer: A straight-chain, four-carbon alkene has two possible structures depending on where the double bond sits: but-1-ene, CH2=CH-CH2-CH3 (double bond between the first and second carbon), and but-2-ene, CH3-CH=CH-CH3 (double bond between the second and third carbon).

questions.topic: Saturated vs unsaturated carbon compound - identification test and combustion
questions.question: A carbon compound P has six carbon atoms and twelve hydrogen atoms (C6H12). (a) Is P a saturated or unsaturated carbon compound? Justify your answer by drawing/describing a possible structural formula. (b) Describe a chemical test that can be used to determine whether compound P is saturated or unsaturated. (c) Name the products formed on burning compound P in excess air.

rubric.point: With the formula C6H12, P could be either a saturated cyclic compound (a cycloalkane, e.g. cyclohexane, which has one ring so needs 2 fewer H than a straight-chain alkane) or an unsaturated straight-chain compound (an alkene, e.g. 2-hexene) - both formulas are C6H12, so the compound is ambiguous from formula alone and both are acceptable structures

Test: add a few drops of bromine water to the compound - unsaturated compounds decolourise bromine water (addition reaction) rapidly even in the dark, while saturated compounds do not react with it under these conditions
Burning in excess (sufficient) air gives complete combustion, producing carbon dioxide and water as the only products

questions.model_answer: The molecular formula C6H12 alone does not fix whether P is saturated or unsaturated: it matches both a saturated ring compound like cyclohexane (a cycloalkane, which has two fewer hydrogens than the straight-chain alkane of the same carbon count because forming the ring uses up one bonding position on each end carbon) and an unsaturated open-chain compound like 2-hexene (an alkene, whose C=C double bond likewise removes two hydrogens compared to the saturated chain). To decide which P actually is, the standard test is to add bromine water to it: an unsaturated compound decolourises the orange-brown bromine water quickly (via an addition reaction across the double bond) even without light, whereas a saturated compound shows no such reaction. When burnt in excess air, any carbon compound like P undergoes complete combustion, producing only carbon dioxide and water.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Diamond is a good conductor of electricity.
Reason (R): In diamond, every carbon atom is covalently bonded to four other carbon atoms, using up all its valence electrons in bonding.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
questions.explanation: A is false: diamond does not conduct electricity - it is actually an excellent electrical insulator. R is true: each carbon atom in diamond forms four strong covalent bonds to neighbouring carbon atoms, leaving no free (delocalised) electrons or ions available to carry an electric current - which is precisely why diamond does not conduct electricity (unlike graphite, another carbon allotrope, which does conduct because it has one delocalised electron per carbon atom).

questions.topic: How soap molecules clean - micelle formation
questions.question: A soap molecule has a hydrophilic (water-attracting) ionic head and a long hydrophobic (water-repelling) hydrocarbon tail. Explain how this structure allows soap to remove oily dirt from clothes, referring to the formation of micelles.

rubric.point: When soap is mixed with water containing oily/greasy dirt, the hydrophobic tails of soap molecules point into (dissolve in) the oil droplet, while the hydrophilic ionic heads remain on the outside, in contact with the surrounding water

This arrangement forms a spherical cluster called a micelle, with the oily dirt trapped at the centre; since the micelle's outer surface is ionic/hydrophilic, the whole cluster stays suspended (dispersed) in water and can be rinsed away, effectively lifting the dirt off the fabric

questions.model_answer: Soap molecules have an ionic (hydrophilic) head that is attracted to water, and a long hydrocarbon (hydrophobic) tail that is attracted to oils/greases but repelled by water. When soap is used on oily dirt in the presence of water, the hydrophobic tails of many soap molecules bury themselves into the oil droplet (dissolving into it), while their ionic heads remain on the outside, facing and interacting with the surrounding water. This arrangement forms a spherical structure called a micelle, with the oily dirt trapped at its centre and an ionic, water-friendly surface on the outside. Because the outside of the micelle is hydrophilic, the whole cluster - dirt and all - stays suspended in the water rather than clinging to the fabric, allowing it to be rinsed away, which is how soap lifts oily dirt off clothes.
